Physical Regulator Installation

Alignment Selection

Select how the regulator is mounted. Mount the device squarely with wires pointing downward — the built-in accelerometer uses this orientation as its reference so it can report accurate heel, pitch, and passage comfort metrics. (Small residual tilt is corrected by the Zero Now button below.)

Level offsets (none stored): ℹ️ Press Zero Now with the boat at rest in calm water. The regulator stores its present attitude as level, so heel and pitch read zero there. Repeat after any remount. Reading now shows live heel and pitch with the offsets applied, and reads near zero after a good capture.
Reading now: —

Location in Vessel

Approximate positions are acceptable. These measurements help improve motion analysis accuracy.

Distance from Centerline (feet):

Height Above Waterline (feet)
Positive = above waterline, Negative = below, 0 = at waterline
Saves to this regulator immediately. If the regulator is registered for cloud features, the boat record uploads within about a minute, once the field is off. Changing boat equipment or type can move you into a new leaderboard group. A new mounting position affects new data only.

Steps

Progress is saved on the regulator, so it survives a page reload and shows the same on any device. The badge on the right of each step shows its state: ✓ DONE = finished, ▶ = the step you're on (RUNNING while the wizard is open, RESUME when paused), ○ = not yet run. Tick the steps to run, then press the button below — coupled steps are selected automatically.

Only the ticked steps will run.

Charge Rate:

Physical Panel Override is on, so the charge rate is set by the switch on data Cable 3 pin 5 — switch on is High, switch off is Low — and these buttons only show which mode that switch has chosen. Turn the override off under Setup → System → Security & Maintenance to set the rate from here.

Tachometer Keep-Alive — Automatic Learning ℹ️On: the regulator learns where the alternator begins making current at each speed and keeps the Keep-Alive (%) column a small margin below it. Off: edit the column by hand.
Automatic Learning (?): ℹ️On: the regulator fills in the Keep-Alive (%) column. Off: you edit the column.
Off On
Margin Below Onset (%) (?): ℹ️How far below the current-onset point to set the floor. Larger = safer (never forces unwanted current), smaller = field stays more primed.
Onset Delta (A) (?): ℹ️How far current must rise above zero during learning to count as the alternator starting to make current. Usually under 1 A, a few times the sensor noise.
Re-arm Current (A) (?): ℹ️If this much current appears at a learned floor, the floor is lowered one margin step. Set above the current sensor's zero drift, a couple of amps.
Step Dwell (s) (?): ℹ️How long RPM, temperature, and field must hold steady at each learning step before the next step. A few seconds is enough.
Probe Step (%) (?): ℹ️How many field-duty points each learning step climbs. Smaller is more exact but slower.
Temperature Compensation (?): ℹ️On: the floor is corrected for alternator temperature, lower when cold and higher when hot. Off: learned floors apply as they are.
Off On
Reference Temperature (°F) (?): ℹ️The alternator temperature the learned floors are based on. About 180 °F is typical, since learning happens hot.
Maximum Floor (%) (?): ℹ️No learned floor can exceed this, even during learning.
Steady Band — RPM (%) (?): ℹ️How much RPM may wander and still count as steady. Tighter = stricter.
Steady Band — Temperature (°F) (?): ℹ️How much temperature may wander and still count as steady.
Steady Band — Field (%) (?): ℹ️How much the applied field may wander and still count as steady.
Per-RPM Learning Status ℹ️Live view per RPM range: the floor in use, the learned current-onset point, how confident the learning is (0–100%), and how long since that range was last confirmed. "Active" marks the range being observed right now.
RPM Floor (%) Onset (%) Locked Learn °F Last seen

No calibration data yet — run the Keep-Alive Floor commissioning step (Setup ▸ Alternator ▸ Commissioning) to measure the per-RPM onset floors.
Current RPM Index: ℹ️Which RPM table row (0–9) the regulator is using now, based on engine speed. −1 means no RPM reading yet. 0

Output Control
Field Control (?): ℹ️ Auto runs the charge stages and all protections. Manual drives the field directly from the Manual Field PWM box below and turns off most protections, including temperature, engine speed, battery, and current control. The On/Off switch, the hardware over-voltage shutdown, and the field ceiling stay active. If the battery monitor is not reading, Manual has no over-voltage protection. Switching to Manual asks for confirmation and lists everything that turns off.
Manual Field PWM (%) (?): ℹ️Field duty applied in Manual mode, 0–100%. Only Max Field %, Max Field Volts and the two board ceilings limit it. No effect in Auto mode. Use with caution: Manual mode bypasses the thermal, engine-speed, battery, and current protections.
Min Field (%) (?): ℹ️Lowest field duty held anywhere while charging in Auto mode, which keeps a stator-driven tachometer reading. Usually better set per engine speed in the RPM table's Keep-Alive (%) column, leaving this at or near zero. The banner reads MIN FIELD when this floor is setting output.
Max Field (%) (?):limiting ℹ️Highest field duty allowed in every mode. Set no higher than 99%, because the field drive can overheat at 100%. The lowest of this, Max Field Volts, and the two board ceilings below applies, and that one is marked "limiting".
Max Field Volts (V) (?, ?% now):limiting ℹ️Highest average voltage applied to the field winding. Many 24 V, 36 V, and 48 V alternators use a 12 V field winding, and this protects it. Field Winding Voltage in Vessel Info sets this. Change it here only to match a different rating on the alternator's datasheet. The lowest of this, Max Field (%), and the two board ceilings below applies, and that one is marked "limiting".
Field Current Ceiling, 10 A (?% now):limiting ℹ️Not a setting. The duty at which estimated field current reaches the board's 10 A rating at the present system voltage. Its accuracy depends on Field Resistance.
Field Drive Heat Ceiling (?% now):limiting ℹ️Not a setting. The highest duty that keeps the regulator's field-drive parts within their temperature rating right now. It falls as the regulator warms, and a cooler mounting location raises it.
Min RPM For Field (RPM) (?): ℹ️ In Auto mode, the field cuts when engine speed reads below this value, about 40 ms after the first low reading (160 ms at most). 0 removes this cut, but a tach reading of zero still turns the field off. To charge without a working tach, ignore engine speed under Setup → System → Run Without Failed Sensors.
Field Resistance (Ω) (?, ?): ℹ️Resistance of the field circuit: rotor winding, brushes, slip rings, field wire, and fuse. Measure runs the field resistance test with the engine off. The field-current estimate, the 10 A limit, and the drive-heat protection all use this value. An ohmmeter reading through the brushes reads high and lets the field run harder than those limits intend, so enter only a test result, with the alternator temperature the test showed. A 12 V system with no battery shunt can skip the test, and 2 Ω is then used.
at °F
Field Wiring (?): ℹ️How the field is wired at the green field connector: the 1-3 jumper is P-type, the 2-4 jumper is N-type.
Field Switching Freq (Hz) (?): ℹ️100 to 2000 Hz is a good range, may want to avoid human hearing frequencies depending on installation location and noise.
Warmup Ramp Rate (A/s) (?): ℹ️ Rate at which the output current ceiling rises from 0A each time the alternator enables. Set to 0 to disable (immediate full output). Example: 2 A/s reaches 120A cap in 60 seconds.
Rate Limiting
Setpoint Rise Rate (A/s) (?): ℹ️Maximum rate the current target can increase in Auto mode. Does not apply during on/off transitions, only Duty Ramp Rate applies then. Use a slower rate (e.g. 5 A/s) to prevent sudden demand spikes.
Setpoint slew limiter (?): ℹ️ On: the current target ramps at the Setpoint Rise and Fall rates above. Off: the target steps instantly (not recommended).
Off On
Big-Step Threshold (A) (?): ℹ️When the current target jumps more than this many amps above the present target, the climb uses the slower Big-Step Rise Rate, which helps prevent overshoot trips. Set high to disable.
Big-Step Rise Rate (A/s) (?): ℹ️Slower rise rate used for large jumps in the current target. Keep below Setpoint Rise Rate.
Setpoint Fall Rate (A/s) (?): ℹ️Maximum rate the current target can decrease in Auto mode. No effect during on/off transitions, only Duty Ramp Rate applies then.
D-term brake fall rate (A/s) (?): ℹ️Faster fall rate used while the voltage damper (D term) is reducing current during a fast voltage rise. A value below Setpoint Fall Rate is raised to match it.
Startup Rise Rate (A/s) (?): ℹ️Current-target rise rate used only when charging first starts in Auto mode. A slow value, such as 3 A/s, lets the alternator build field current gradually and avoids an over-voltage trip at startup.
Duty Ramp Rate (%/s) (?): ℹ️Maximum rate of duty cycle change in ALL cases including on/off transitions. Lower values prevent rapid field changes that can disturb the tachometer signal.
Shutdown Final Ramp Rate (%/s) (?): ℹ️Slowest rate allowed during the shutdown ramp, so the field reaches 0%. Lower is easier on the tachometer signal but makes shutdown longer.
Shutdown Phase 2 Hold Time (ms) (?): ℹ️How long to hold at minimum field duty before beginning slow ramp to 0. Set to 0 to skip Phase 2 entirely.
Shutdown Ramp Time (s) (?): ℹ️How quickly the field winds down after the alternator is switched off. This is the time for the field to fall by about two-thirds. Below about 4 s, engine speed can falsely read zero for a few seconds after switch-off. 0 uses the Final Ramp Rate for the whole ramp.
No-Output Current (A) (?): ℹ️Alternator current at or below this counts as making no output. Raise it if the alternator current sensor reads a few amps with the field off.
Temperature Settings
Alternator Temp Limit (°F) (?): ℹ️ Maximum safe temperature at the sensor location. The regulator begins reducing current as temperature approaches this value. Hard warning and critical shutdowns trigger above it. Sensors often read 20–30°F cooler than true winding temperature, account for this offset when setting this value.
Temp Warning Excess (°F) (?): ℹ️️Degrees above the Alternator Temp Limit that trigger a warning. Output ramps to zero and charging locks out for a time. If the temperature stays this high for the Temp Sustained Timeout, the field is cut.
Temp Critical Excess (°F) (?): ℹ️️Degrees above the Alternator Temp Limit that cut the field immediately.
Temp Sustained Timeout (s) (?): ℹ️️Seconds at warning temperature before a shutdown that ramps output to zero and cuts the field. The timer resets if temperature drops below the warning level.
Temp Source (?): ℹ️The temperature sensor used for thermal protection. Digital uses a digital probe (DS18B20). Thermistor uses an analog thermistor, set up with the values below.
Internal Temp Offset (°F) (?): ℹ️ONLY used for alternator component life physics models. How much hotter windings, bearings, brushes are than physically measured alternator case temperature. Typical: 40–60°F (22–33°C).
Thermistor Series Resistor R_fixed (Ω) (?): ℹ️Value (Ω) of the fixed series resistor in the thermistor voltage divider circuit. Must match the resistor physically installed on the board.
Thermistor Beta (?): ℹ️Beta coefficient from the thermistor datasheet, characterizes how its resistance changes with temperature. Typical NTC thermistors: 3000–4000. Find the exact value in your thermistor's datasheet.
Thermistor Reference Temp T0 (°C) (?): ℹ️Reference temperature (°C) at which the thermistor's nominal resistance is specified. Almost always 25°C per datasheet.
Current Sensing
Hall Effect Sensor Range (?): ℹ️Select the rated current range of your QNHCK1-21 clamp-on hall effect sensor. Choosing the wrong range will scale all alternator current readings incorrectly.
Invert Alternator Amps (?): ℹ️Reverses the sign of the raw alternator current reading. Enable if your hall-effect sensor is mounted with reversed polarity and reports negative amps during normal charging.
No Yes
Alternator Current Offset (A) (?): ℹ️Amps subtracted from every alternator current reading to cancel the sensor's zero error. Measured Zero below sets it, or enter a known value.
Current Threshold (A) (?): ℹ️Below this, the Alternator is assumed OFF. Affects many alternator calcs.
Alternator Zero Correction (?): ℹ️The current sensor never reads exactly zero with no current flowing, and the error shifts with temperature. On: the regulator learns that error from readings taken while the alternator is idle and subtracts it, up to 3 A. It stays on "learning" until it sees a wide temperature swing, which normally takes a run and a cooldown. Reset Zero starts over.
Off On
Fit: —
Measured Zero: ℹ️Measures the current sensor's zero error so it can be stored as the Alternator Current Offset. Zero Now turns the field off, averages the reading for ten seconds, and reports the result. Apply stores it. Measure while the engine compartment is warm. With the engine running, charging pauses for under a minute.
—
Zero-Drift Log (?): ℹ️The readings the zero correction learns from, taken while the alternator isn't charging. With this off the correction has nothing to learn from. Download CSV saves the readings. Reset Log erases them.
Off On
Records: —
Alternator Health
Set Alternator Life Manually (%) (?): ℹ️This will adjust life for brushes, bearings, insulation all together, meant for zeroing all together.
CV Mode holds the alternator output to a fixed user-specified voltage target, bypassing the normal Bulk / Absorption / Float charge algorithm. The voltage loop adjusts the current setpoint on every output-current control update (about every 13 ms, up to ~30 ms worst case) through Voltage Loop Kp; its integral term (Voltage Loop Ki), which eliminates steady-state voltage error, steps once per Voltage Loop Interval (about every 105 ms at the default 100 ms, up to ~125 ms). All current limits remain fully active — RPM Cap Table, thermal penalty, Fast OV, Load Dump, the Group 3 iExcess detectors, the Group 4 battery charge limit, and any user overrides — so the only thing this mode changes is the voltage target. Use this tab to tune voltage loop parameters or simulate a fixed-voltage regulator. ⚠️ Not intended for lithium batteries.
CV Mode On/Off (?): ℹ️ Not safe for Lithium batteries. This mode bypasses the normal charge algorithm, use only with flooded or AGM batteries, or in consultation with your battery manufacturer.

Overrides normal charging with fixed voltage control, mainly useful for tuning voltage loop parameters or simulating an old-school automotive alternator voltage regulator.
Off On
Target Voltage Setpoint (V) (?): ℹ️ Voltage target when mode is enabled.
Shortcut to CV tuning mode →

Pick a pill to focus on one protection. Tune the control loops first (in the Tuning tab, protections off), then adjust these after.

View:

Group 4 (Battery Limit) and Group 5 (Load Dump) both act on measured battery current, and no battery shunt is installed — so their pills and parameters are greyed. They arm themselves the moment a shunt is fitted under Setup → Battery → Measurement Sources.

Enable
G0 Group 0 Enable (?) ℹ️Master switch for the last-resort over-current trip, which turns the field off when alternator current exceeds the Command Limit plus 10 A. Stays armed even when Protections is off. Leave it on except during bench diagnostics.
Off On
G1 Group 1 Enable (?) ℹ️Master switch for the predictive over-voltage layer (Group 1). Off: that layer never engages, and all other protections still work. Turn off if heavy belt ripple causes false trips.
Off On
G2 Group 2 Enable (?) ℹ️Master switch for the measured over-voltage layer (Group 2), the main voltage protection. Over-voltage damages every battery chemistry. Leave this on.
Off On
G3 Group 3 Enable (?) ℹ️Master switch for both alternator over-current detectors (Group 3). Off: only these detectors stop, and all other protections stay armed.
Off On
G4 Group 4 Enable (?) ℹ️Master switch for the Battery Charge Current Limit (Group 4), the cap on charging current into the battery. Off removes only that cap.
Off On
G5 Group 5 Enable (?) ℹ️Master switch for the Load Dump trip (Group 5), which catches a large load dropping off the bus while charging. Stays armed even when Protections is off. Leave this on.
Off On
RPM Tach Plausibility Cut (?) ℹ️Cuts the field when the tach shows the engine turning and the regulator is driving the field, but the alternator delivers nothing for several seconds. That means a false RPM reading, a failed alternator, or an open field circuit. Left running, a false reading can drain the battery through the field with the engine stopped. Stays armed even when Protections is off. Leave this on.
Off On
Detection

When measured alternator current exceeds the safe limit for the debounce duration, the trip fires. Set Command Limit to the lowest safe maximum on the alternator side of the system — alternator continuous rating, mechanical belt drive capacity, fuse ratings, and wiring limits. Whichever is lowest. Battery acceptance is handled separately by the Group 4 Battery Charge Current Limit. The trip threshold is automatically 10 A above Command Limit.

Predicts where battery voltage will be a fraction of a second from now: predicted = measured + Prediction Horizon × voltage rise rate. Engages when the prediction exceeds the active charge target by more than the Group 1 Trigger Margin. dvdt EMA TC sets how much the rise rate is smoothed before prediction — larger TC means smoother but laggier. Group 1 Enable (in the Enable section above) turns the whole layer off.

Engages when measured battery voltage exceeds the active charge target by more than the Group 2 Trigger Margin. Group 2 Enable (in the Enable section above) turns the whole layer off. Above this proportional shed sits the Over-Voltage Ladder card: two timed cut tiers that fire only when the filtered voltage stays over their trip lines continuously for their set time to act, then the absolute software and hardware instant cuts.

Watches alternator output current. Two regimes, split at the Strict Over-Current Band below the active voltage target. Near the target — the voltage-limited (CV) phase: engages when the time-averaged current rises above the moving current setpoint by more than the Detection Threshold — the sloped trip line set by Slope and CV base below. Below the band — the current-limited (bulk / CC) phase: the looser Detection Threshold (Bulk) takes over — the same line raised by CC offset and judged against the commanded ceiling instead of the moving setpoint, so normal speed-up ramps toward the ceiling don't false-trip. Both thresholds are bounded by the Threshold Floor / Ceiling (amps); Averaging Time Constant sets how heavily the current is smoothed before each comparison, and Release Hysteresis sets the re-arm point.

Battery Charge Current Limit is a ceiling, not a trip: the commanded alternator current is capped at the limit plus the measured house-load draw, so the battery never sees more than the set amps no matter what the loads are doing. It needs the INA228 battery shunt and is off when set to 0.

Load Dump catches a large load dropping off the bus while the alternator is charging: the current that load drew surges into the battery as a rising spike in battery current, sharp when a FET switches the load off and spread over a few readings when relay contacts open. Three tiered thresholds sit on the rate-of-change of battery current, each firing when its set number of consecutive samples all exceed its threshold. A battery disconnecting under charge drives battery current toward zero instead; the over-voltage protections (Groups 1–2 and the Over-Voltage Ladder) catch that event. Fewer samples act faster on a single spike; more samples reject noise but wait longer. A sample is one battery-current reading, taken about every 6 ms (up to ~18 ms worst case), and the output is cut at the next control update, about 13 ms apart (up to ~30 ms worst case) — each tier's resulting time to act is shown under its sample count. Unlike the over-current detectors, Load Dump stays armed even when test protections are disabled — only the Group 5 Enable toggle in the Enable section disarms it.

V
Over-Voltage Ladder ℹ️The battery-voltage cuts, lowest to highest: two timed cuts, the software shutdown, and the hardware shutdown. Brief excursions get time to settle with no cut. Anything sustained is cut before a battery BMS would open its charge path. Keep them in that order, with the low tier at or above the Group 2 margin.
Timed Cut LOW — Margin Above Target (V) (?)
V
Timed Cut LOW — Time to Act (ms) (?) ℹ️How long the filtered battery voltage must stay continuously above the low-tier trip line before the field is cut. Any dip back under the line restarts the clock. 0 disables this tier.
ms

V
Timed Cut MID — Time to Act (ms) (?) ℹ️How long the filtered battery voltage must stay above the mid-tier trip line before the field is cut. Any dip under the line restarts the clock. 0 disables this tier.
ms
Alternator Hard Shutdown Voltage (V) (?) ℹ️Battery voltage at which the field is cut instantly, in every mode including Manual. The re-enable delay grows if the cut repeats. Set it 0.1 V per 12 V of system voltage below the Hardware Shutdown Voltage.
V
Hardware Shutdown Voltage (V) (?) ℹ️A voltage limit inside the battery monitor chip that cuts the field electrically, with no software involved. It is the backstop if software hangs and should never be the one that fires. Set it 0.2 V per 12 V of system voltage below the battery BMS's charge-disconnect voltage. For lead-acid and AGM, set it where connected DC equipment becomes the limit.
V
G4 Battery Charge Current Limit (A) (?) ℹ️The most charging current the battery may receive, such as its C-rate limit. The alternator can still supply house loads on top of this. Requires the battery shunt. 0 disables the limit.

The shunt also measures solar, shore power, and DC-DC chargers, so the alternator backs off to make room for them, down to zero if they cover the whole limit.

Response

The field drive FET is switched off and the field collapses through the coil's natural time constant. The only knob is the trip debounce above; none of the integrator-bleed actions used by the other protections apply here.

KHard — Response Slope sets how aggressively the current cap is trimmed per volt of overshoot — recomputed from the live overshoot every tick. Shared with Measured OV. AW Bleed Rate continuously drains the voltage integrator while any of the other protections is clamping.

Same KHard — Response Slope cap-trim mechanism as Predictive OV (shared parameter). AW Bleed Rate continuously drains the voltage integrator while the clamp is active.

Trims the current cap by the measured amount of excess each tick — the same cap-trim action the OV groups apply, but driven by alternator-current overshoot rather than voltage. K_bleed — Integrator Bleed Mode additionally drains the voltage integrator when the event fires — 0 means snap to zero (maximum response); > 0 takes a single bite proportional to the amount of excess. AW Bleed Rate also drains continuously while active.

Battery Charge Current Limit has no trip response — it is a ceiling the command simply never exceeds.

Load Dump snaps the voltage integrator to 0 instantly on the rising edge of the trip — hardcoded, no adjustable parameter for the snap itself. AW Bleed Rate drains the integrator continuously while it is active.

G1G2 KHard — Response Slope (A/V) (?)
A/V
G3 K_bleed — Integrator Bleed Mode (?) ℹ️How the voltage loop's stored current is reduced when an over-current event (Group 3) fires. 0 drops it to zero, the fastest response. Above 0 reduces it in proportion to the overage, which causes less voltage dip. Try 2–5 if the voltage dips too far.
A
G1G2G3G5 AW Bleed Rate (×Table/s) (?) ℹ️How fast the voltage loop's stored current is reduced while a protection is active, as a fraction of the Alternator Current Limit per second.
×Table/s
Recovery

After the trip, the regulator enters a ramp-and-lockout — the field stays at 0 until the over-current condition has cleared. The recovery path used by the other protections (Recovery Seed Fraction, Seed Protect Window) is not used here.

When all protections have released, the controller's stored current memory (the voltage-loop integrator) is restored to pre-event value × Recovery Seed Fraction. Seed Protect Window protects the fresh seed from being immediately drained by a brief subsequent event. Fast Setpoint Rise Rate then accelerates the slewed current setpoint back up while battery voltage is comfortably below target, so the alternator crosses its deadband and starts producing current again quickly. Two independent helpers speed the rest of the return — Recovery Refill rebuilds the stored current memory faster in proportion to what is missing, while Recovery Boost is an instant proportional bridge (P-boost) that scales up the loop's immediate corrective push while the bus is below target. Both pace themselves off live voltage error and taper away as the battery reaches target (Load Dump excepted; it re-asserts on its own). Smart Reseed corrects the restored current when the event was caused by a load switching off, and Load Pickup Boost applies the refill's fast rebuild to ordinary load steps outside protection events — both use the battery shunt's measurement.

G1G2G3 Recovery Refill — rebuild the stored current memory (?) ℹ️After a protection event, the voltage loop's stored current restarts at a fraction of its earlier value. On: it rebuilds faster, paced by voltage error. Off: it rebuilds at the normal rate.
Off On
G1G2G3 Max Refill Speed (×) (?) ℹ️How fast the stored current rebuilds right after a protection event, with Recovery Refill on. Higher restores charging sooner, lower is gentler.
×
G1G2G3 Load Pickup Boost — serve new loads at the refill rate (?) ℹ️On: when a load switches on while holding a voltage target, the alternator picks it up faster, so the battery does not carry it for many seconds. Off: the alternator picks up the load at the normal pace. Requires a battery shunt.
Off On
G1G2G3G5 Recovery Seed Fraction (?) ℹ️After a protection trip clears, charging current restarts at this fraction of what was flowing before. Used with a battery shunt. The No-Shunt fraction below is used without one.
×
G1G2G3G5 Recovery Seed Fraction, No Shunt (?) ℹ️Restart fraction used with no battery shunt. A low value takes a few seconds longer to climb back. A high value risks a repeat trip after a load dump.
×
G1G2G3G5 Recovery Climb Rate (?) ℹ️How fast charging current climbs back after a protection trip, as a fraction of alternator maximum per second. 0.20 on a 100 A alternator is 20 A per second. The climb pauses as voltage nears target, so a fast rate does not overshoot.
×max/s
G1G2G3G5 Smart Reseed — subtract loads that switched off (?) ℹ️On: when a large load switching off causes a trip, the regulator subtracts that load from the restored current and lowers the restart further on a repeat trip. Off: every restart uses the plain seed fraction. Measuring the load needs a battery shunt.
Off On
G1G2G3 Recovery Boost — faster climb out of the hole (?) ℹ️On: while battery voltage is below the charge target, the alternator drives extra current to raise voltage faster, easing off near target. Off: the return to target runs at the normal pace.
Off On
G1G2G3 Recovery Boost — Max Strength (×) (?) ℹ️How hard the recovery boost pushes when voltage is far below target. Higher climbs faster, but too high can trigger another over-voltage trip. 1× disables the boost.
×
G1G2G3 Recovery Boost — Full-Strength Shortfall (V) (?) ℹ️How far below target voltage must be for the boost to reach full strength. Lower reaches full strength sooner. Entered per 12 V and scaled for 24 V, 36 V, and 48 V.
V
G1G2G3 Recovery Boost — Dead Area Below Target (V) (?) ℹ️A zone just below target where the boost stays off, so ripple and small wobbles are not boosted. Larger leaves more dips at normal speed. 0 boosts from the first shortfall. Entered per 12 V and scaled for 24 V, 36 V, and 48 V.
V
G1G2G3G5 Deep Recovery Band (V) (?) ℹ️How far below target voltage must be for recovery to count as deep, which speeds up the current climb. Smaller speeds up sooner but risks a repeat trip. Entered per 12 V and scaled for 24 V, 36 V, and 48 V.
V
G1G2G3G5 Deep Recovery — Climb Speed Multiplier (×) (?) ℹ️How much faster the current climb runs when voltage is past the Deep Recovery Band. Too high can overshoot. 1 disables the speed-up.
×
G1G2G3G5 Recovery Arrival Flare — Band (V) (?) ℹ️Within this many volts of target, the restored current tapers down, so voltage arrives at target without pushing over the trip line. Wider is gentler but slower. 0 disables it. Entered per 12 V and scaled for 24 V, 36 V, and 48 V.
V
G1G2G3G5 Recovery Arrival Flare — Floor (×) (?) ℹ️How much restored current is still allowed when voltage reaches target, as a fraction of the recovery goal. Lower gives more protection against a repeat trip but can let voltage dip briefly under a large load. 1 disables the taper.
×
G1G2G3G5 Seed Protect Window (ms) (?) ℹ️How long after the voltage loop's stored current is set that the AW Bleed Rate is held off, so a brief new protection event does not immediately drain it. 0 disables this.
ms
G1G2G3G5 Fast Setpoint Rise Rate (×) (?) ℹ️Multiplier on Setpoint Rise Rate for a short time after a protection releases, so current returns quickly while voltage is still under target.
×
G1G2G3G5 Fast Rise Window (ms) (?) ℹ️Longest time the faster rise can last after a protection releases. It normally ends sooner, when voltage climbs into the headroom band. Range 500–30000.
ms
G1G2G3G5 Fast Rise Headroom (V) (?) ℹ️Volts below the charge target at which the faster rise stops and the normal Setpoint Rise Rate resumes. Keep inside the Strict Over-Current Band. Range 0.05–2.0 V.
V
G1G2 Field Drain Time (ms) (?) ℹ️How long the field takes to fade after a cut, until output falls to 10%. Commissioning measures this across engine speed, and this value is the longest of those times. Editing it replaces the measurement with one value at every speed.
ms

Test Parameters

Test Type (?): ℹ️ Sine Sweep (recommended) varies the field across the frequencies set below with the control loop off and measures how the alternator responds. Step moves the field up and down and reads the response time.
⚠️ Protections: ℹ️Enabled: all protections run normally.

Disabled: the over-voltage and over-current protections that would fight the test are bypassed. Load Dump, the hardware over-voltage shutdown, and the hard over-current trip stay active.

Re-enable before normal use. A red banner shows while protections are disabled, and the setting returns to Enabled on reboot.
Disabled Enabled
Wave Floor (A) (?): ℹ️ Alternator output the test settles at before the sweep, and the low point of the wave. Raise it if the wave clips near zero at low RPM. Keep it within what the alternator can make at the test RPM.
Wave Amplitude (% duty) (?): ℹ️ Size of the duty change during the test. Larger gives a cleaner signal but disturbs the system more. Must be large enough to see clearly above noise.
Sweep Start (Hz) (?): ℹ️ Lowest frequency in the sine sweep. The sweep is log-spaced from here up to Sweep End. Lower frequencies take longer (each point holds for a fixed number of cycles). 0.5 Hz is a sensible low end.
Sweep End (Hz) (?): ℹ️ Highest frequency in the sweep, keep below about 25 Hz. A higher setting is trimmed automatically to what the current readings support.
Cycles per Frequency (?): ℹ️ Sine cycles measured at each frequency. More cycles reduce noise but lengthen the test.

Apply Results

The test measures the field coil's electrical lag (plant delay). The "Set All Filters" button inside the modal writes plant/3 to the alternator-current PID feedback filter and the full plant delay to the voltage filter — see each tooltip below for the reasoning. You can also override any value individually.

Output current PID feedback filter (ms) (?): ℹ️ Smoothing on the alternator current reading used by the current control loop. Set All Filters writes this from the measured plant delay. Shorter reacts faster, longer reduces noise.
Voltage sensor smoothing filter (ms) (?): ℹ️ Smoothing on the measured battery voltage, used for the rise-rate calculation and charge stage decisions. Set All Filters writes this from the measured plant delay. The voltage loop and the over-voltage checks do not use this filter.
Plant Delay — the measured electrical lag between a field duty command and the resulting current response. Run the test at a steady speed within your normal operating range. Both alternator-current filters take roughly 1/3 of the plant delay: the PID feedback filter needs that to stay inside its control loop without stacking two equal lags and eroding phase margin, and the on-screen current display gets the same value to stay responsive. The voltage filter isn't in a tight control loop, so it takes the full plant delay. See each filter's tooltip above for the full reasoning.

Controller Parameters
ℹ️Zeroes the current loop's stored output. Field duty ramps back up from 0. Use if manual tuning has left it wound up.
PID Kp (Proportional) (?): ℹ️Immediate response to current error. Higher = faster correction but more overshoot. Start with 0.3, increase if too slow, decrease if oscillating. Commissioning measures this gain for the alternator it is wired to.
PID Ki (Integral) (?): ℹ️Eliminates steady-state error over time. Higher = faster elimination of offset but may cause instability. Start with 0.5, increase slowly if needed. Commissioning measures this gain for the alternator it is wired to.
PID Kd (Derivative) (?): ℹ️Dampens rapid changes to reduce overshoot. Usually kept at or near zero.
Oscillation Damper (?): ℹ️Detects a slow wobble in field drive (0.3 to 2 Hz) at steady engine speed, then tests one fix at a time. A fix that measurably shrinks the wobble is kept for that engine speed. Off: full strength always, and the learned map is kept but not applied.
Off On

Shortcut to the damper's status, speed map and episode record →

Damped Gain (% of PID Ki) (?): ℹ️The gain the damper cuts to during a test and across a known trouble spot, as a percentage of PID Ki. Lower is softer, higher makes a real improvement harder to confirm.
Required Improvement (%) (?): ℹ️How much the wobble must shrink for the test's fix to be kept. Higher demands stronger proof, but a real trouble spot may take longer to confirm.
Pocket Edge Taper (% of speed) (?): ℹ️How far past each end of a trouble spot the reduced strength tapers back to full, as a percentage of engine speed.
Retest Cooldown (min) (?): ℹ️How long the damper waits after a failed test before testing again.
Speed Steadiness (%) (?): ℹ️How steady engine speed must hold during detection and testing, as a percentage. Drift beyond this cancels the test.
Detection Confirm Scans (?): ℹ️How many scans in a row, one every 1.6 seconds, must agree a wobble is present before a test starts. More is slower but surer.
Detection Amplitude (?%): ℹ️How large the swing in field duty must be to count as a wobble. Lower it if the regulator visibly surges but the damper never reacts. Raise it if tests keep starting on other disturbances.
PID Sample Divisor (?): ℹ️The output current PID normally updates on every fresh current sample. A 2 makes it update every other sample, etc. Don't adjust.
PID Tracking Gain (1/s) (?): ℹ️Keeps the current loop from running ahead of the field when a limit is holding output back. Higher corrects faster. 0 disables this. Active only when Ki is above 0.
Signal Source (?) — alternator current (ADS1115): ℹ️How the alternator current reading is smoothed before the current control loop uses it. EMA: smooth average, set on the Plant Delay tab. MA(N): average of N readings. Raw: no smoothing.
MA Window — N samples (?): ℹ️Number of alternator current readings averaged for MA(N). Readings arrive about every 13 ms (up to ~30 ms), so N=2 is about 26 ms.
Output current PID feedback filter (ms) (?): ℹ️Smoothing on the alternator current reading used by this loop. Set in Tuning → Plant Delay.
Read-only — set in Tuning → Plant Delay

Controller Parameters
Gain selection
CV Gain Source (?): ℹ️How Voltage Loop Kp and Ki are set. Measured calculates them from the battery response found in Voltage Control Autotuning, using the two settings below. Manual uses the values you type. Switching does not erase the other's values.
Manual Measured
Active gains: — ℹ️The Kp and Ki the voltage loop is using now, in 12 V-equivalent units, after the battery-temperature correction.
No fit yet — run the Voltage Control Autotuning step in commissioning. Until then the voltage loop runs safe default gains. ℹ️The battery response measured in Voltage Control Autotuning and the gains calculated from it, before temperature correction. Re-run that step to update it.
CV Aggressiveness (α) (?):  ℹ️How strongly the voltage loop corrects when CV Gain Source is Measured. Lower is gentler and more damped, higher corrects harder but risks overshoot. Takes effect without re-commissioning.
CV auto-tune Ki/Kp ratio ρ (?): ℹ️How strong the slow correction is compared to the fast one when CV Gain Source is Measured. Lower is gentler, higher risks overshoot. Takes effect without re-commissioning.
Voltage Loop Kp (A/V) (?): ℹ️Voltage loop fast response: amps of current target per volt of error. Higher reacts harder. Works the same on 12, 24, 36, and 48 V banks.
Voltage Loop Ki (?): ℹ️Voltage loop slow correction, which pulls battery voltage exactly to target over time. Higher reaches target faster, but too high causes overshoot. Large lithium banks may need more. 0 turns it off. Works the same on 12, 24, 36, and 48 V banks.
Voltage D term (rate-of-rise damping)
Damping strength (Kd) is set automatically from the voltage loop's proportional gain (Kp) — Kd = Td × Kp — so it scales with the same battery measurement that sets Kp. Switch CV Gain Source to Manual to set it yourself. The value in use is on the Active gains line above. ℹ️With CV Gain Source set to Measured, Kd is calculated from Kp. Set CV Gain Source to Manual to enter Kd directly.
Voltage Loop Kd (?) ℹ️Voltage damper strength: amps trimmed from the current target per V/s of voltage rise beyond the tolerance. Slows a fast approach to target so it does not overshoot into the protections, with no field cut. Too high slightly slows the final approach. Works the same on 12, 24, 36, and 48 V banks.
Voltage for D term filter (ms) (?) ℹ️Smoothing on the battery voltage before the damper measures its rate of rise. Longer rejects belt ripple and noise but sees a fast rise later. 0 uses the raw voltage.
Voltage-Rise Tolerance base — V/s at zero amps (?) 10s peak rise rate: — ℹ️Voltage-rise rate at zero amps below which the damper does nothing. Lower catches gentler approaches but gets closer to ripple, higher leaves more to the protections. Commissioning sets this from measured ripple. The readout shows the fastest rise in the last 10 seconds.
Voltage-Rise Tolerance slope — V/s per amp (?) ℹ️How fast the tolerance rises with commanded current. Commissioning sets this from measured ripple. 0 makes the tolerance flat.
Voltage-Rise Tolerance floor — minimum V/s (?) ℹ️The lowest the tolerance can go, in V/s, so belt ripple does not engage the damper.
Voltage-Rise Tolerance ceiling — maximum V/s (?) ℹ️The highest the tolerance can go, in V/s, so a real fast rise still engages the damper. At the Slope Ceiling or above, the damper is effectively off.
Safety Margin — V/s above measured ripple slope (?) ℹ️How far the tolerance sits above the measured ripple, in V/s. Larger means fewer false engagements but a later reaction to a real fast rise. Applying it sets the base and slope above. Requires the measurement from Commissioning Step 5.
Ripple slope vs. Voltage-Rise Tolerance ℹ️The tolerance line from the settings above, drawn against the ripple-driven voltage rise measured at commissioning. Red shading marks currents where the damper would engage on ordinary ripple. Nothing here changes automatically.

One-Sided (?) ℹ️On: the damper can only remove current during a fast rise. Off: it can also add current on a fast fall while below target.

Off On

Needs a battery temperature. Choose a source under Setup → Battery → Battery Temperature.

Battery-Temp Gain Derate (?): ℹ️A cold battery's internal resistance rises, which makes the voltage loop more aggressive. On: the regulator scales Kp and Ki for battery temperature to keep the response consistent. Off: commissioned gains are used at all temperatures. Needs a measured battery temperature.
Off On

The battery-temperature gain derate is Off, so the commissioned gains run unchanged at every temperature and the coefficient below has no effect. Turn the derate on above to use it.

Not yet commissioned — run the Voltage Control Autotuning step.
Battery-Temp Resistance Coefficient (?): ℹ️How strongly the gain correction reacts to temperature: the battery's fractional change in resistance per °C below 25 °C, so 0.024 is 2.4%/°C. Higher is stronger, 0 makes it inactive.
Target voltage ramp
Target voltage ramp — up rate (V/s) (?): ℹ️How fast the charge target can rise, as in Bulk to Absorption. 0 makes the change instant.
Target voltage ramp — down rate (V/s) (?): ℹ️How fast the charge target can fall, as in Absorption to Float. An instant drop can trip over-voltage protection and cut the field. Ramping lets current ease off instead. 0 makes the change instant. Hard shutdown is not affected.
Target voltage slew limiter (?): ℹ️ On: the charge target moves at the up and down rates above. Off: the target changes instantly, which can trip over-voltage protection when it drops (not recommended).
Off On
Setpoint drop wind-down
Enable wind-down (?): ℹ️ On: when the voltage target is lowered, the regulator steps current down at the rate below until voltage reaches the new target, usually in a few seconds with no protection event. Off: the voltage loop and target ramp handle the drop. Protections stay armed either way.
Off On
Wind-down rate (fraction of max amps/s) (?): ℹ️How fast current steps down after the target is lowered, as a fraction of alternator maximum per second. Larger is quicker but can dip under the new target, smaller is gentler and slower.
Wind-down stop margin (V) (?): ℹ️The step-down stops when voltage is within this many volts above the new target, and the voltage loop finishes the job. Larger is safer against dipping under the target but slower to finish.
Governors & loop timing
Rise governor / anti-windup limiter (?): ℹ️ On: when the target steps up, the voltage loop acts on only what the current loop can support, which prevents overshoot and an over-voltage trip. Off: the loop acts on the full step and can overshoot (not recommended).
Off On
Field smoothing limiter (duty slew) (?): ℹ️ On: field duty changes only at Duty Ramp Rate, protecting the hardware from harsh transitions. Off: duty steps instantly (not recommended). Same setting as on the Current tab.
Off On
Voltage sensor smoothing filter (ms) (?): ℹ️Smoothing on the measured battery voltage, used for the rise-rate calculation and charge stage decisions. Set in Tuning → Plant Delay.
Read-only — set in Tuning → Plant Delay
Voltage Loop Interval (ms) (?): ℹ️How often the voltage loop's slow correction updates. Shorter responds faster but can amplify noise, longer is smoother but slower to correct. The fast response runs continuously regardless.
Overshoot & OV-recovery shaping
CV Tuning Helpers (?): ℹ️ On: voltage above target drains the slow correction faster, and the voltage damper trims fast rises. Both reduce overshoot and speed over-voltage recovery. Off: the loop runs plain, which is easier to read while tuning Kp and Ki. Turn back on afterward. The over-voltage protections stay active either way.
Off On

Controller Parameters
ℹ️Resets the temperature control loop. It takes about a minute to resume full look-ahead. Use if it is stuck on a bad reading.
Temp PID Kp (A/°F) (?): ℹ️Amps of current reduction per °F over the temperature target. Higher cuts current harder as temperature nears the limit.
Temp PID Ki (?): ℹ️How fast the temperature loop builds and holds its current reduction. Higher responds faster to slow engine-compartment heating.
Below-Setpoint Bleed (× Ki) (?): ℹ️How fast the current reduction releases when temperature is below target, as a fraction of Temp PID Ki. Lower holds it through brief dips, which prevents a growing temperature swing. 1.00 releases as fast as it builds.
Thermal Lookahead (s) (?): ℹ️How far ahead the temperature loop projects the rate of rise, in seconds. Larger reduces current earlier. Too large causes a slow temperature swing around the target. Range 0–300 s.
Thermal Slope Window (s) (?): ℹ️How long a period is used to measure the temperature rate of rise. Shorter reacts faster but reads noisier. Range 10–60 s.
Temp PID Interval (ms) (?): ℹ️How often the temperature control loop runs.
Temp PID Filter Alpha (?): ℹ️Smoothing on the filtered temperature value. With a digital probe, this affects only the logged and plotted value. With a thermistor, smoothing is fixed.

Provokes the over-voltage protection safely at any state of charge: it charges at idle until the battery voltage settles and stops creeping upward (typically 10–45 s), parks the bus at a constant-voltage target it can actually reach (a set headroom below the settled idle voltage, close enough that real charging current keeps flowing), and you snap the throttle to about half max RPM. The response is scored — protection-event count, any hard current-sensor cut, recovery time, and post-recovery stability; overshoot and the recovery dip are reported for context. All protections stay fully active; the firmware ends the run itself. Also the final commissioning wizard step — run it here any time after a tuning change.

Test Parameters

Target Headroom Below Idle (V) (?) ℹ️How far below the settled idle voltage the test sets its voltage target. Smaller leaves more charging current flowing, a harsher test, larger is gentler. Entered as a 12 V value and scaled for 24 V, 36 V, and 48 V.
Stability Limit (V) (?) ℹ️How much battery voltage may swing during the test's setup before the test refuses to run. Loosen it if cycling loads such as a fridge or autopilot keep voltage moving. Entered as a 12 V value and scaled for 24 V, 36 V, and 48 V.

PID Control Architecture

Three-Loop Cascaded Control: Three independent controllers react at different rates and stack on top of each other. The output current loop runs on every fresh alternator-current sample (about 75 times a second: every 13 ms or so, up to ~30 ms worst case) and drives the alternator field duty cycle to chase a current target. The voltage loop recomputes its proportional and damping terms on that same update and steps its integral about 10 times a second (about every 105 ms at the default Voltage Loop Interval, up to ~125 ms) during the voltage-hold phases (Absorption and Float) — it computes the current target that holds the battery at the configured voltage. In the current-limited phase (Bulk) the voltage loop stands aside and the system charges at the ceiling. The temperature loop also runs on every control update, but its alternator temperature reading refreshes only about every 5 seconds (default OneWire probe); it outputs a single thermal penalty in amps that gets subtracted from the RPM Cap Table ceiling before the inner loops see it. The cascade is strict: temperature constrains what current the voltage loop is allowed to ask for; the voltage loop constrains what the output current loop is allowed to chase; the output current loop is the only thing that touches the field. Each layer never reaches past the one below it.

RPM Cap Table: For each engine RPM range, you configure a hard ceiling based on your installation's physical limits — belt load, shaft stress, alternator and battery bank ratings. This ceiling is enforced after the thermal penalty is applied and is never exceeded regardless of thermal state. The ceiling can be entered as either a current limit (Amps mode) or a power limit (kW mode) using the toggle above the table. In Amps mode the configured value is a fixed current ceiling. In kW mode the regulator divides your power limit by live battery voltage on every control tick to derive the amp ceiling — so the mechanical load on the belt and shaft stays constant regardless of voltage sag or rise during charging.

Forecasted Thermal Penalty: The temperature controller acts on the higher of two temperatures: the present filtered reading, and a projected temperature — present temperature plus the measured rate of rise multiplied by the Thermal Lookahead horizon. Projection is what lets the loop pull current down before the alternator actually reaches the limit, while taking the higher of the two means a hot alternator is never given current back just because the temperature trend has flattened. The setpoint is the real damage limit (Alternator Temp Limit) and the output is a penalty in amps: zero means no restriction, higher numbers mean more current pulled away from what the RPM Cap Table would otherwise allow. Because the penalty is relative rather than absolute, it transfers cleanly across RPM and stage changes. The penalty itself is slew-limited so brief temperature noise doesn't cause harsh current swings.

Voltage Loop: A proportional-integral controller (Voltage Loop Kp and Ki) holds battery voltage at target during the voltage-hold phases (Absorption and Float). Its output is an alternator-current target, capped at the RPM Cap Table ceiling (with thermal derating) and, when the Group 4 Battery Charge Current Limit is set, at that limit plus the measured house-load draw — so the battery's share of the output is bounded regardless of what the loads are doing. The current-limited phase (Bulk) commands alternator current the same way. The integrator uses asymmetric gain — it bleeds down fast when voltage runs above target and rises slowly when below, biasing toward safety. A deadbanded derivative term (Voltage Kd) trims current straight out of the command when voltage is climbing quickly, which checks overshoot during the approach to target. Anti-windup freezes upward integration whenever the current ceiling — not voltage — is the binding constraint, so the integrator does not load up while unable to act. The loop gains are set by the commissioning wizard's autotuning rather than tuned by hand (see below), and can be automatically re-scaled with the measured battery temperature to hold the loop's speed and damping constant as the battery's internal resistance changes with temperature.

Three-Stage Charging: The regulator implements a constant-current / constant-voltage / float charging cycle (CC/CV/Float), with an optional Idle mode after Absorption for lithium longevity.

In Bulk, the voltage loop is off and the system charges at the maximum thermally allowed current from the RPM Cap Table. This continues until battery voltage has been held at the Bulk Voltage target continuously for the Bulk Voltage Debounce Time — a debounce that prevents transient voltage spikes from triggering a premature transition.

In Absorption, the voltage loop engages and holds the battery at the Absorption Voltage. The battery itself now dictates how much current it accepts — current tapers naturally as the battery fills. The system exits Absorption when charge current has dropped to or below the Tail Current for the Absorption Completion Time, confirming the battery is genuinely full. If the system is thermally constrained — meaning the thermal penalty is meaningfully active AND current is already near the Tail Current — tail detection is suspended until thermal headroom recovers, preventing a false exit before the battery is truly full. A safety timeout (Absorption Timeout) forces a transition to Float (or Idle, if Use Float is Off) if Tail Current is never reached.

In Float, the voltage loop holds the battery at the lower Float Voltage. After the Minimum Float Time has elapsed, the system monitors for voltage sag or sustained discharge current. If either condition persists for the Rebulk Debounce Time, or if Float Duration expires, Bulk charging restarts — subject to SoC blocking if SoC data is available. If Use Float is Off, the system skips Float entirely and enters Idle after Absorption, charging again only when rebulk criteria are met.

Independent Protection Layers: Several fast-response protections sit outside the three-loop cascade and act on raw sensor readings without filter lag. Fast OV (Groups 1 and 2) caps current immediately when raw battery voltage runs above a margin below the charging target. Load Dump protection (Group 5) caps current when a sustained battery-current rise rate is detected, catching FET disconnect or load drop events. The over-current detector (iExcess, Group 3) caps the current ceiling when measured alternator current overshoots the commanded setpoint — with a strict regime near the voltage target and a looser one in bulk — and collapses the voltage-loop integrator at the same time so it can't immediately re-demand the excess. Its trip threshold is not a single fixed number: it is max(floor, percent·commanded current, ceiling), so the percentage term rides up with the commanded current — tight at low current (catches real over-current sooner) and looser under heavy output (tolerates the larger legitimate ripple that comes with load) — while the floor guards the low-command case and the ceiling caps it. You set those in Protections; the commissioning wizard measures the ripple and plots it against your thresholds so you can check them, but never sets them for you. None of these depend on the control loops being active — they are always armed.

Stability and Recovery: All mode transitions are bumpless — both the output current loop integrator and the voltage loop integrator are seeded to the operating point before the new mode takes over, so transitions never produce a setpoint step. If the temperature sensor goes stale, the temperature loop holds its last penalty value and re-enters smoothly when fresh data returns rather than snapping back. Anti-windup keeps the temperature integrator parked near any tighter non-thermal constraint when thermals are not the binding limit, so the penalty can climb the instant temperature demands it. A hardware-level shutdown path (GPIO4) provides two independent escape hatches: immediate cut for critical conditions (temperature critically over limit, hard fault) and a controlled ramp-then-cut for sustained warning-level conditions. GPIO4 protection remains active regardless of loop state. Any fault that interrupts charging restarts from Bulk when charging resumes, never mid-cycle.

How the Control Loops Are Tuned

Start with commissioning — it does nearly all of this for you. The Commissioning tab runs a guided wizard that measures your specific alternator and battery bank and sets almost every loop and protection parameter automatically. You creep the throttle when it asks and confirm each step; it does the math. On most installs this is the only tuning you ever do — the manual procedure below is for hand-verifying or fine-tuning after the wizard, or for the rare case where you want to override what it found.

The wizard walks nine steps, each writing real settings on Apply:

• Prep — snapshots your current settings and checks preconditions (engine running, headroom, a valid battery shunt) so a run can be reviewed or reverted.
• Field curve — ramps field duty open-loop and maps duty→output current, finding the saturation knee.
• Current Control Autotuning — a sine sweep on field duty measures the inner current loop's plant (time constant and gain) and proposes its PID gains and filter constants (also on the Plant Delay tab).
• Verify Current Control — a closed-loop sweep with the new inner-loop gains, confirming the loop is stable before anything downstream trusts it.
• Disturbances — you creep idle→cruise while it records the worst ripple per RPM range (belt resonance) on both the alternator and battery signals, building the Resonance & Ripple Map.
• Fault Threshold Autotuning — sets the over-current detector's trip line from the ripple just measured: the line runs a Safety Margin above the ripple and is drawn against the measured points so you can confirm it clears them. It writes straight to the Protections settings — adjust the margin or the individual values by hand if you like.
• Voltage Control Autotuning — commands one bounded current pulse through the tuned inner loop and measures how battery voltage responds to the current step (the finite-horizon gain K20), then computes the voltage-loop gains from your chosen response time.
• Keep-Alive Floor & Field Decay — at each of three held speeds (max working → mid → idle) it finds the field onset point, filling the per-RPM Keep-Alive (%) column, then cuts the field once and times the alternator-current drain at that speed; the three drain points fit the speed-dependent line the over-voltage response's field-drain timing reads.
• Stress Test — charges at idle until the battery voltage settles, parks the bus at a constant-voltage target it can actually reach, then you snap the throttle to about half max RPM so the over-voltage protection fires on a reachable setpoint; the protection response and recovery are graded, with corrective actions offered on a poor result. Writes nothing — a pure acceptance check.

Every step is advisory — it proposes, and nothing changes until you press Apply. You can re-run a single step, or clear and start over. Progress is stored on the regulator, so it survives a reload and looks the same from any device.

Manual tuning (optional). The output current loop and the voltage loop each also have their own live tuning mode you can drive by hand — Tuning Mode for the inner current loop (Current tab), and the CV Gain Source selector (Measured or Manual) on the Voltage tab for the voltage loop. Tune them in that order — inner loop first, then voltage — because each layer depends on the one beneath it being stable. The rest of this section covers hand-tuning the inner current loop; the voltage loop has its own dedicated tab with a built-in step test, a Measured gain source that reuses the commissioned fit, and live scoring. The temperature loop is tuned offline from logged data (no live step test) — its tab shows the live control plot and the controller parameters.

Three-Phase Process: The goal is to tune the core PID first, then verify it handles the rate limiters gracefully with anti-windup tracking. Tune in bulk stage — absorption and float share the same output current loop, so a well-tuned bulk response carries through automatically.

Phase 1 — Core Loop (Unrestricted):
Set both slew limiters to very high values to effectively disable them:
• Setpoint Rise Rate: 1000 A/s
• Setpoint Fall Rate: 1000 A/s
• Duty Ramp Rate: 1000 %/s
Enable Tuning Mode and watch the step response on the plots. Tune Kp, Ki, and Kd until you get well-damped step responses with minimal overshoot (10–20%) and fast settling time (2–4 seconds).

Phase 2 — Actuator Slew + Anti-Windup:
Re-enable the actuator slew limiter by setting Duty Ramp Rate to a realistic value (typically 10–30 %/s). Keep setpoint slew limiters high (1000 A/s). Run tuning mode again and watch for overshoot after transitions. If you see overshoot once the duty ramp catches up, increase PID Tracking Gain until the overshoot disappears. This is the back-calculation gain that bleeds the integrator down whenever the duty output is rate-limited.

Phase 3 — Production Verification:
Set Setpoint Rise Rate and Setpoint Fall Rate to your desired production values (typically 5–20 A/s rise, 20–50 A/s fall). Run tuning mode one final time to verify the loop remains stable and well-behaved with both rate limiters active.

Tuning Philosophy for Cruising:
Run tests at moderate RPM within your typical cruising range. A slower, well-damped loop (4–6 second settling time) is preferable to a fast loop that causes harsh load transitions. The independent protection layers (Fast OV, Load Dump, the Group 3 iExcess detectors, GPIO4 hard cut) handle the unsafe edges — you don't need the loop itself to react instantly. Smooth and stable beats fast and harsh.

Every installation is different — always verify with a step test in your own setup.

Four independent checkpoints decide what data gets recorded on the Live Data → Diag tab. These are their gates & tuning knobs — pick a pill to see only that checkpoint's settings; a setting shared by two checkpoints shows under both of them.

View:

C1 — Anomaly Detection watches the fast current sensor for rectifier/stator fault signatures. It shares the fast channel and its steady-state admission gates (current drift floor/slope, input-range switching) with C2 — those live in the shared Fast Current Channel section. Its own pieces: the fault alarm, the fault-class and lifetime-anomaly readouts, and the anomaly snapshots in the Waveforms flipbook. Arming ignores engine speed entirely, so it keeps working with a dead tach.

C2 — Resonance & Ripple Map learns the strongest current-ripple tones at every engine speed and load, from the same fast channel as C1. It uses the shared current-drift gates plus two gates of its own: the steady-state RPM margin (a window is discarded when the engine sits on a speed-bin edge) and the minimum tone amplitude. Its results: the map itself, the worst ripple & tone table, and the biggest actionable disturbance.

C3 — Charging System Health grades output amps against the best this machine has ever done at the same operating point. A point is admitted only after every signal — RPM, field duty, voltage, temperature, amps — holds steady. Those admission gates and the curve-fit tuning are the knobs under Gates & Tuning in this section; the resulting health gauge, session plot, and engine-hours trend appear on Live Data → Diag → Alternator.

C4 — Ripple Measurements is one measurement engine with two collectors: the RPM ripple table is filled only by the commissioning game, and the ripple-vs-current line on the Protections plots is filled only by Commissioning Step 6. These gates define what counts as a valid measurement for both. They are deliberately separate from C1/C2’s gates, so tuning them can never loosen fault-detector arming.

Go to Plots →

Recorder (idle): ℹ️Records data only, and charging is unaffected. Holds 18.2 minutes, then stops and keeps every row. A console warning appears with one minute left. Press Record, then sweep, change throttle, or run as usual. —
Field sweeper (idle): ℹ️Takes over the field and ramps it up and back down at a fixed rate, so field moves independently of engine speed. Runs with or without a recording. Auto mode only. What’s Activeℹ️Active during a sweep: hardware and software over-voltage shutdowns, timed over-voltage cuts, the hard over-current trip (Group 0), critical alternator temperature, engine speed, current sensor, Max Field %, and the On/Off switch.

Off during a sweep: Group 1 and Group 2 over-voltage limits, current-overshoot trim, load dump detection, the temperature loop, current and voltage limits (the sweep only turns around at them), Min Field % and keep-alive floors, the field rate limit, and charge stages. Ways to stop itℹ️Stop sweep ends the run and eases the field back out. Reverse now sends the up leg back down immediately, at the same rate. The On/Off switch, or anything that turns charging off, ends the run too.
Sweep rate (% field per second): ℹ️Slower is more accurate and takes longer. 1 %/s over a 60-point span takes about two minutes up and back.
Sweep up from (% field): ℹ️Where the up leg starts and the down leg ends. Set below where output begins to build.
Sweep up to (% field): ℹ️Where the up leg turns around, limited by the field ceiling in force now. The sweep usually turns around sooner, at a current or voltage limit.
Turn around this far below a current limit (A): ℹ️How far below a current limit the sweep turns around, because nothing holds output off a limit during a sweep. Never more than a quarter of the limit. 0 turns around on the limit.
Turn around this far below a voltage limit (V): ℹ️How far below a voltage limit the sweep turns around, so it does not end in an over-voltage cut. 0 turns around on the limit.
Min Field (%) (?): ℹ️Same setting as Min Field (%) in Setup → Alternator → Field Control. A sweep ignores it. Everything else obeys it.
Manual Field PWM (%) (?): ℹ️Same setting as Manual Field PWM (%) in Setup → Alternator → Field Control. Applied only in Manual mode, which bypasses the thermal, engine-speed, battery, and current protections. The sweeper needs Auto mode.
Captured session ℹ️Transfer saves the recording as a CSV file and frees the memory. Do this after each run, then press Record again.
Reset / Start Over ℹ️Clears My History, the whole % vs Engine-Hours trend, and session stats, and restarts the engine-hour axis at zero. Tuning settings are kept. Do this after replacing the alternator, regulator, or drive belt. Cannot be undone.
C4
Ripple Measurements
One measurement engine, two collectors: the RPM ripple table is filled only by the commissioning game, and the ripple-vs-current line on the Protections plots only by Commissioning Step 6. These gates define what counts as a valid measurement for both. A measurement counts only if conditions were stationary: the window's two halves must have (nearly) the same average — a throttle or load transient walks the average in one direction and is rejected, while a rough-but-repeating condition (a hunting idle, cycling loads) swings hard yet averages the same in both halves and is admitted. This is deliberate: a "dirty speed" is exactly what the over-current protections experience, so it must make it into the table. Each gate shows its worst value over the last 10 s (green = passing). Never relaxed during commissioning: a stationary number cannot be measured while ramping — the wizard's instructed pauses are when measurements admit.
Capture Window (ms) (?): ℹ️How long each ripple measurement lasts. After changing it, clear the map and re-run the commissioning current check, because measurements at different lengths are not comparable.
Current Drift Floor (A) (?): ℹ️Drift allowed during a ripple measurement. The current command may move no more than the larger of this or the slope % below. Each line shows worst value minus limit over the last 10 s, and zero or below passes. alt mean-shift beyond limit (larger of Floor / ¼ window swing), 10s worst, ≤0 passes: — batt mean-shift beyond limit (larger of Floor / ¼ window swing), 10s worst, ≤0 passes: —
Current Drift Slope (%) (?): ℹ️Companion to the floor above, as a percent of mean alternator current. Applies to the current command only. command travel beyond limit (larger of Floor / Slope % × mean), 10s worst, ≤0 passes: —
Steady-State RPM: ℹ️Engine speed must also hold steady during the measurement. The limit is automatic. A negative reading means inside the limit. RPM mean-shift beyond limit (larger of 10 RPM / ¼ window swing), 10s worst, ≤0 passes: —
Engine & Alternator Parameters
RPM Scaling Factor (?): ℹ️ Scales the tachometer signal into engine RPM. Adjust until the RPM shown here matches your engine's tachometer. Changing it erases every table and record measured against the old RPM axis, on the device and in the cloud, and requires re-commissioning. The alternator must be off.
Pulley Ratio, Alt to Engine (?): ℹ️ *** Only used for Alternator Lifetime Calcs *** Alternator RPM = Engine RPM × this ratio. Common: 2.0-3.0
Ignition Override (?): ℹ️ Off: the regulator counts the ignition as on only while the key is on, and charges only then. On: it counts the ignition as on all the time, so charging no longer waits for the key; the alternator switch turns it on and off. Use On when no ignition wire is connected. With it on, the regulator also stays fully awake with the engine off, so it draws more power while the boat sits.
Off On

Fuel Consumption ℹ️Fuel burn rate at each engine speed, with straight lines between points. Up to ten points. Leave trailing rows at zero to use fewer.

Engine SpeedRPM ℹ️Engine speed breakpoint. Values must increase down the column. Leave trailing rows at 0 to use fewer than ten points. Fuel Burngal/hr ℹ️Burn rate at that engine speed. Measure it, or take it from the engine manufacturer's fuel curve.

Phase Definitions

No battery shunt is wired to the regulator, so zero-current float and Force "Maintain Mode" are greyed below. Both need the regulator's own shunt, set up under Setup → Battery → Measurement Sources.

Tail Current and the Rebulk Current Threshold are greyed too, because no battery monitor is set up under Setup → Integrations either. Absorption ends on time alone, and float (if enabled) then holds the float voltage.

Bulk Phase
Bulk Voltage (V) (?):
ℹ️ 14.4V typical.
Bulk Voltage Debounce Time (sec) (?): ℹ️ How long battery voltage must remain continuously within 50 mV below Bulk voltage (or higher) before Absorption begins. Prevents transient voltage spikes from triggering an early Absorption entry. 0.25s typical. Note that there isn't any controls difference between Bulk and Absorb other than the limiting voltage, if those are set differently, so this is more a question of display nomenclature.
Absorption Phase
Absorption Voltage (V) (?): ℹ️ Voltage held during Absorption. Typically 0.1 to 0.2 below Bulk Voltage for an AC charger/ solar or 0.3 to 0.4 below for an alternator controller. It's wise to leave some margin for transients during rapid engine speed changes. The battery dictates how much current it accepts, current tapers naturally as the battery fills.
Tail Current (A) (?): ℹ️ Absorption ends when charging current tapers to or below this value continuously for the Absorption Completion Time. Confirms the battery is full. 5 amps per 100Ah of bank is typical. The battery must also still be up at the Absorption Voltage, because a big load or the engine dropping to idle can pull charging current down to almost nothing while the battery is only part full.
Absorption Completion Time (sec) (?): ℹ️ How long current must remain at or below Tail Current before Absorption ends. Prevents a momentary current dip from triggering a premature exit. 10-60s typical.
Absorption Timeout (min) (?): ℹ️ Maximum time in Absorption before forcing a transition regardless of current. Safety fallback in case Tail Current is never reached. Typical starting point: 30m per 100Ah of battery bank. This clock only runs while the battery is held up at the Absorption Voltage, and the phase always ends at twice this figure of real elapsed time, not counting time when the alternator is not charging or a followed charge voltage limit holds the battery below the Absorption Voltage.
Float Phase
Float Mode (?): ℹ️ No Float (idle): after Absorption the field turns off, and charging restarts when the rebulk criteria are met.

Voltage Float: holds the battery at Float Voltage, returning to Bulk when the rebulk criteria are met or Float Duration runs out.

Zero-Current Float: the alternator carries the house loads and the battery rests at 0 A. Needs the battery shunt.

Float Voltage and Float Duration only apply to the Voltage Float mode selected above. Pick Voltage Float to set them.

Float Voltage (V) (?):
ℹ️ Holding voltage used only in Voltage Float mode. Typical: ~13.4V
Float Duration (hrs) (?): ℹ️ Maximum time in Float before returning to Bulk.
Minimum Float Time (min) (?): ℹ️ Delay after Absorption completes before a voltage or discharge-current rebulk is allowed. Applies in all three Float Modes (idle, voltage float, zero-current float). A state of charge at or below SoC Allow Rebulk Below rebulks without waiting.

Physical Panel Override is on, so Force "Maintain Mode" is set by the switch on data Cable 3 pin 7, and this toggle only shows what that switch has chosen. Turn the override off under Setup → System → Security & Maintenance to set it from here.

Force "Maintain Mode" (?): ℹ️ Targets 0A net battery current- this is not a recommended mode, as errors may build up over time.
Off On
Charge Start / Rebulk Criteria
Rebulk Voltage (V) (?): ℹ️ If battery voltage drops below this threshold during Float or Idle, and stays there for Rebulk Debounce Time, the system returns to Bulk. 13V typical.
Rebulk Current Threshold (A) (?): ℹ️ If net battery current is more negative than this value (i.e. the battery is discharging at this rate or faster), the system returns to Bulk. Provides more reliable rebulk detection than voltage alone under load. 2 to 5 amps per 100Ah of battery bank is typical.
Rebulk Debounce Time (sec) (?): ℹ️ How long the rebulk condition (voltage sag or discharge current) must persist continuously before a return to Bulk is triggered. Prevents nuisance rebulk from transient loads. 10-60s typical.
Safety

Sensor cross-checks that stop charging when the two voltage readings disagree, plus the shared shutdown-timing knobs (fault lockout duration, settle time before the field is cut). The over-voltage cut thresholds — the timed cut tiers, the Alternator Hard Shutdown Voltage, and the Hardware Shutdown Voltage — live together in the Over-Voltage Ladder card under Setup → Alternator → Protections → Detection.

Shortcut to the Over-Voltage Ladder →

Voltage Disagree Threshold (V) (?): ℹ️Voltage difference between the two battery voltage readings that indicates sensor disagreement. Helps detect wiring or sensor issues. Typical: 0.15V.
Voltage Disagree Timeout (s) (?): ℹ️How long voltage disagreement must persist before triggering warning. Filters transient differences.
Field Collapse Delay (s) (?): ℹ️How long charging stays off after a fault that ramps the field down, even if the fault clears. Applies to voltage sensor, temperature, and current sensor faults.
Settle Time Before Cut (ms) (?): ℹ️How long duty must be at 0% before the field enable turns off. Prevents relay chatter during brief dips. Typical: 500ms.
Battery Temperature
Battery Temperature Source (?): ℹ️Which measurement the regulator uses as battery temperature. Automatic takes the first available: battery probe, NMEA 2000, VE.Direct, then RV-C. Not fitted means the boat has none, so the lockouts stay off. With any other choice, charging stops if the reading stops arriving.
No battery temperature available

Needs a battery temperature. Choose a source under Setup → Battery → Battery Temperature. Without one, charging below freezing is left to the battery's own BMS, and a BMS disconnect while charging can spike system voltage.

Cold-Charge Lockout (?): ℹ️ On: charging stops while battery temperature is below Min Charge Temp, the alarm sounds if alarms are enabled, and charging resumes about 2 °F above it. Off: charging continues at any temperature (not recommended for lithium, which is permanently damaged by charging below freezing).
Off On
Min Charge Temp (°F) (?): ℹ️ Below this battery temperature, the Cold-Charge Lockout stops charging. Set it at the battery's cutoff, usually 32 °F for lithium. Has no effect unless the lockout is on.
Hot-Charge Lockout (?): ℹ️ On: charging stops while battery temperature is above Max Charge Temp, the alarm sounds if alarms are enabled, and charging resumes about 2 °F below it. Off: charging continues regardless of battery temperature.
Off On
Max Charge Temp (°F) (?): ℹ️ Above this battery temperature, the Hot-Charge Lockout stops charging. Set it at the battery manufacturer's maximum charge temperature. Has no effect unless the lockout is on.
SoC Integration

State of charge needs a battery shunt wired to the regulator or a battery monitor set up under Setup → Integrations. Neither is present, so this card is greyed and no state of charge is reported.

SoC Info Available? (?) ℹ️ If the regulator is hooked up to a battery shunt per the installation directions and you select Yes, SoC is used to reduce unnecessary rebulk cycles near full. If OFF, charger ignores SoC.
No Yes
SoC Block Rebulk Above (%) (?): ℹ️ Suggest 90%. If SoC is at or above this value, rebulk is blocked even if voltage or current drop below the rebulk trigger thresholds. Prevents nuisance stage resets when the battery is already near full. Must be at least 10–15% higher than SoC Allow Rebulk.
SoC Allow Rebulk Below (%) (?): ℹ️ Suggest 75%. If SoC falls below this value, rebulk is forced regardless of the block threshold or float timer. When the battery has depleted, a full bulk charge should always run. Should be at least 10–15% below SoC Block Rebulk to prevent hunting between stages.
